title: From Model to Classroom: Evaluating Generated MCQs for Portuguese with Narrative and Difficulty Concerns
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether current generative AI models can produce usable multiple-choice questions (MCQs) for Portuguese elementary reading comprehension, especially questions targeting narrative elements and varying difficulty levels. The authors are motivated by the practical challenge of creating high-quality MCQs for classroom use and by the lack of evidence about how AI-generated questions perform in real educational settings, particularly outside English. The study asks whether generated MCQs are acceptable to experts, how their psychometric properties compare with human-authored items, and whether model-assigned difficulty aligns with expert and student performance.

The intervention is an AI-based MCQ generation pipeline applied to Portuguese narrative texts. The authors compare three generation approaches: GPT-4o in a one-step zero-shot prompting setup, Gemma-2-27B in a similar one-step setup, and a two-step method combining a fine-tuned ptt5-v2-large model for wh-question generation with Gemma-2 for answer options and difficulty annotation. Generated MCQs are evaluated against human-authored MCQs from Porto Editora materials. Evaluation includes expert review of item quality (well-formedness, narrative alignment, option clarity, answerability, plausibility, and perceived difficulty) and quantitative psychometric analysis of student responses using classical test theory metrics such as difficulty and discrimination.

The population and context are Portuguese elementary school students and education professionals. Expert review involved 18 native Portuguese-speaking participants with professional expertise in Portuguese language education, including teachers and publishing professionals. Student testing involved 284 students across 14 classes in a school group in the Valongo region of Portugal, using grade-appropriate reading materials for 2nd to 4th year elementary education. The study took place in authentic school classrooms, with paper-based administration under teacher supervision.

The main conclusion is that large language model-generated MCQs, especially from GPT-4o and Gemma-2, are broadly comparable to human-authored MCQs in overall quality, though they still exhibit issues with semantic clarity, answerability, and distractor design. Human-authored MCQs were slightly more difficult, more discriminative, and had distractors that engaged students somewhat better, but differences were generally not statistically significant. The two-step ptt5-v2+Gemma-2 method performed worse, especially on answerability and distractor reliability. Overall, the authors conclude that current LLMs can generate classroom-relevant Portuguese reading-comprehension MCQs of comparable quality to human-authored items, but careful validation remains necessary before classroom deployment.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a structured comparative empirical study with expert review and classroom psychometric validation in elementary schools, but it is not a randomized trial of student learning outcomes and is currently an arXiv preprint under review. It fits a quasi-experimental/validation evidence level with meaningful empirical methods but some credibility concerns.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but mixed evidence: generated MCQs were broadly comparable to human-authored ones, yet no clear student-learning effect sizes were reported and some quality dimensions favored human-authored items. Impact is therefore operationally promising but substantively unclear for student outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI for automatic multiple-choice question generation in Portuguese reading comprehension, producing curriculum-aligned narrative-element and difficulty-controlled MCQs for elementary students and comparing them with human-authored items.

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluated reading-comprehension MCQ quality for elementary Portuguese language assessment rather than a learning intervention on students' writing or literacy growth. Expert review found LLM-generated MCQs broadly comparable to human-authored ones on several quality dimensions, and psychometric analysis of student responses (14 classes; 284 students, with 124 validated MCQs and about 45 responses per MCQ) showed no statistically significant differences in estimated item difficulty (Kruskal-Wallis H=1.249, p=0.741) or discrimination (reported H=0.854, p>0.05), though human-authored items were slightly more difficult and discriminative and had better distractor engagement.
finding.measure: Expert review of MCQ well-formedness, narrative alignment, option clarity, answerability, distractor plausibility, perceived difficulty; student-response psychometrics for reading-comprehension MCQs (difficulty 1-P, discrimination D, distractor usage, 3-rule option-quality test)
finding.study_size: n=284 students; 18 expert reviewers; 124 validated MCQs used in student testing

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions generative MCQ generation as a way to reduce the time and cost of manually authoring reading-comprehension assessments, and empirical comparison suggests current LLMs can generate items of comparable overall quality to human-authored ones after validation. However, because generated items still exhibited semantic clarity, answerability, and distractor-quality problems, the efficiency gains appear contingent on expert screening rather than fully autonomous deployment.
finding.measure: Comparative item-generation quality relative to human-authored MCQs as a proxy for feasibility of automating assessment authoring
finding.study_size: 18 expert reviewers; 180 MCQs in expert review, 124 validated MCQs in student psychometric analysis
